title: Opinions and advice on developing a game using AI
author: HazeInsanity
selftext: I would like to ask more veteran devs how to go about developing a game. There's still a big anti AI sentiment on the internet and It might make it harder to build a community. I have no money to hire artists since I'm a college student so I have been using AI. Sometimes I spend entire days just so a single piece of art comes out the right way (coherent with everything else I alredy have and with my vision intact). Slotbound had success despite using AI art but It still makes me wonder the best way to go about it. I'm really enjoying the process of directing and creating a game but I'm a bit scared to share it with others considering the amount of hate you get for using AI. I will start working on January since I have now finished my uni course. I'll earn around 1300 euros every month after taxes, would I be able to afford legit artists considering I also gotta save money for a car and eventually a house down payment? What would my best shot be?

Just start. The hardest part.

replies.author: HazeInsanity
replies.body: I have started, I was simply unsure about which direction to take.  Thanks for the advice

replies.author: roychr
replies.body: My honest take here is that contrary to the wave of people coming in and thinking they have a shot at it alone, u/Such--Balance said it right, the most important thing is to start. Unfortunately you have to be conservative in what you put on screen, this requires knowledge of how shaders work, how to do orthogonal views, how bones work and how animations interpolate. Should you have started during the Quake2 and Quake3 mod scene years you would by now have an immense know how on how we did things with not much back in the days. I work today with people that are senior in the game dev industry that for example have used Unreal to make AAA gameplay stuff that is awesome but knows jack shit what a PSO is or how many triangle a mesh should have and how you should make up textures in such a way that it worked with cell phones like the IPhone 2-3. Most people did not do manual flash animations using Adobe software and never programmed in actionscript nor knew the joys of making the pip boy menu in Scaleform. This is a deep archive of know how that only curious devs have, others treat their job as a day job. So if you want to start now the AI is a great tool but its a sword and with it you can go out and cut meat in different ways some crude and effective, other cuts beautiful with years of practiced art and dedication. Sharpen your know how, learn how to be a D&D master for story telling and game design, play board games and educate yourself on all sorts of metrics, take the time to take a look at how verticality work in level design, I mean I could go on for a couple of chapters on how each role in a dev team can be simulated by AI but unfortunately you will have to spend lots of time and dedication as you would have anyway to get what we call "the level of execution" that AI cant give you alone. There are no shortcut to this, it requires sacrifice, dedication and a willingness to finish what you started. I worked 10 years at BGS with legendary people now at Gearbox and I can tell you that what makes a great game developer is not the ability to know the latest C++ standard by heart, it is the dedication to make the greatest entertainment software to bring joy and happiness to people. You have a story to tell, go out there and tell it, make sure it reflects who you are and put everything you have in it and then you'll have a shot. Good luck !

replies.author: HazeInsanity
replies.body:
I am making a 2D game inspired by slay the spire but with a really big twist on the combat. I was really unsure about how to go about animations, whether to use bones or not for idle animations, I'm still trying to figure out if breathing + other simple animations are good enough for an idle animation. The point is I have never had this much fun in my life, I'm truly enjoying creating this game of mine even if It is an extremely long and tough journey. I have learned so much since I first started last month and I don't plan to stop. I'm letting my intuition as a long time gamer guide me and then have AI execute it. My plan has always been to make a product worthy of my and other people's time. I'm willing to put in the time and effort to achieve that. I was unsure about being able to create a community around a game that uses AI but you guys have showed me there's nothing to fear and that I should focus on making something good.

Thank you truly for taking the time to spread some wisdom and help me out. Hope to see you around!

comments.author: MaksRengi
comments.body:
Dont spend your car money on artists before you know people want the game. Use AI for now, make the gameplay acutally fun, put up a steam page and see if people wishlist it. If it gets traction, spend the money on a capsule from a real artist first. Its one of the most important things for the hook, its the first thing people see on Steam.

  
About the hate, most players dont care if the game is fun and the art looks consistent. People hate on AI slop no on AI. Just disclose it on steam like youre supposed to and move on

replies.author: HazeInsanity
replies.body: My priority has always been quality over quantity. The advice about the capsule and steam page is really good advice, I'll definitely take note of that. Thank you so much for the encouragement!

comments.author: DeanRayGames
comments.body:
if you are spending all day on one piece of art to iterate and make sure it's coherent and fits well with all your other art, you're doing it right. 

As for the anti-AI haters, they will hate, and there's no amount of quality you can bring to them that will change that. 

But that's not the vast majority of people. The vast majority of people want to play a good game that looks good and is fun to play. 

If you can afford to hire "legit artists" to do art for you game, then do it. It will potentially widen the pool of people who are willing to give your game a try. But remember, game development is a hobby, like any other. It's not a viable plan to make a living. So spend money on it like you would any other hobby, something you enjoy doing for the passion of it. 

I'm not an experienced dev, but I have been "vibe coding" projects for a good bit of time now, and this is the advice I'd give to you. I hope you find it helpful!

replies.author: HazeInsanity
replies.body:
Thanks for the point of view.

My priority has always been to make a good polished game and not a quick buck. I wanted to make something that would be worthy of my and other's time. Game dev has become my main hobby over the last month, It's so addicting.

I found your advice extremely helpful, It truly has motivated me to keep pursuing my dream of publishing a good game regardless of AI or not. Hope to see you around!

comments.author: SadMangonel
comments.body:
Thats for you to figure out. 

Break it down and you'll realise that the question yiure asking cannot be answered.

Ai or no Ai doenst matter. Youre creating a product for consumers. Its up to you to decide whats going to work and gain more profit - either use ai, be done faster and alienate a bunch of "no ai" consumers. Or not.

Or maybe you just dont have a profitable pitch at all right now. Because if the game youre developing is another rpg-light with some basic mechanics, a coop friend game or a wonky farming simulator the sad Story is that theres 5000 of them released a month.

You earn 1300€ after university?? Wtf where are you

As for your question.
Build the game without assets, when it's finished either hire an artist or buy/ build the assets. 
Before even starting, plan the hell out of it. The better the plan the more context ai has to work with. Planning planning planning

All the AI hate was discouraging me a little bit, but you guys have showed me It can work if done right. Thanks for that!

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
But it's not the concept that you need. You have to plan the system in detail, not just the content but the technical part. 

For example: you have an idea for a great game that includes a massive forest. How do you achieve that with good performance? 
A lot of trees are a problem and there are technical solutions. 
When I say plan the game, that's what I mean. Yes you have a nice concept but before starting, think about how you could even reach this goal. And discuss it with your ai. 

As for your job, I'm sorry to hear that, do you speak other languages?

comments.author: adolphite
comments.body:
Don't be scared of nobody. Do what you can do. I legit wouldn't have been able to create a game had it not been the rise of AI. comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: You're in college - this is literally the time for you to start learning how to fill in all of the gaps in your knowledge and skill base. You think AI is going somewhere? Who cares about AI sentiment right now, we're in the singularity, buddy. Nobody knows what the world is going to look like in 6 months let alone 2 or 3 years. You're in a transformational period in history. For the first time in ever there are super intelligences that aren't human being created on the fly that answer and do any intellectual task for pennies to a few dollars. The most important skill you can learn is how to use them to do pretty much anything you have in your head. If they're not good at it now they will be soon, but what they don't really have is any ambition or drive or agency to start a project on their own like you do, and then the taste and discernment to keep it going until finished (maybe this will be solved, who knows, but it's not solved yet). The biggest skills you should be honing right now - the understanding of what project to start and bring to completion, and how to build an audience and get eyeballs on your project in the midst of millions of other people doing the same thing.

replies.author: HazeInsanity
replies.body: This is pretty true. Most people's first games are learning experiences and mine is no exception. I have become much better at using and understanding AI than I was a month ago. I have been doing a lot of research about indie video game marketing including those made with AI art. What I had a hard time finding info about was how to grow a community of people with interest in your AI game. Most of you guys have been telling me most people don't mind AI if it looks and plays good.  I will take your advice to heart. Thank you truly for taking the time to help out!

comments.author: pehmeateemu
comments.body: I suggest you study game development a bit. Learn a bit about how the game systems work. What makes a game good and fun to play. Design the core loop first, test it, polish it, refine it, until you wholly enjoy it. A well designed core loop carries the game. Additional systems around the core loop won't save the game if the core loop is boring. 3D models cost money to commission, rigged and animated ones even more. We're talking from couple hundred euros up per model. 2D can be a bit cheaper. It really depends a lot on complexity and detail. Avoid fiverr (they scalp the artists) and source your artists from Reddit. You will probably need a 100€+ tier subscription if you want to steamroll development. Especially late into production when your codebase is bigger and you want the LLM to chase down bugs through the code. 20€ tier subscriptions will burn through 5h limits with a few prompts when using a stronger model (I would argue almost necessary to catch the harder to pin down bugs). Early the better tier sub gets you more built per day. It's doable but it will be tight.

replies.author: pehmeateemu
replies.body: Card art puts you in a better situation money-wise. Commissioning smaller pieces (eg. 800*600px) in larger lumps allows you to negotiate a better price per piece although you'd be paying more at a time. Agreeing on a set price and receiving the artwork in batches helps you balance money (200-300€ per 4-6 pieces) and the artist their workload. I know someone who I've been working with and they could give you an offer, they've created some dark fantasy pieces for me. Send me dm if you want more info.

comments.author: Careless_Road8873
comments.body:
I'm doing the same thing, a medieval RPG made with AI art, Claude doing most of the code. A few things I learned the hard way.

Put it out early, even rough. My first players found things I would never have found myself, and every round of feedback made the game better. A free browser build on itch costs nothing and tells you fast if anyone cares.

Consistency matters more than quality. Early on players called out a grainy, noisy texture in some pictures as "looks AI". Once I made everything clean and in one style, that mostly stopped. Pick a style and kill anything that doesn't fit, even if it took you a day.

Say you used AI on the page. People who hate it will leave either way, the rest stop looking for it.

Keep the money. Spend it on a capsule artist only when people actually play and wishlist. Until then the game is the thing that has to work, not the art.

Most importantly, you really need to enjoy playing it. Its been a few months now, and i enjoyed playing the game i am developing since the first minute.

replies.author: HazeInsanity
replies.body:
How did you go about finding people willing to try out your game and give feedback on it? I'm not sure where to look.

I have found myself redesigning a lot of the art in my game for that exact reason, I want everything to look coherent and polished.

Thank you very much for the advice, glad to see there are others like me on the same path!

replies.author: Careless_Road8873
replies.body:
Reddit mostly. I posted the browser build in a few dev and itch subs and asked for honest feedback, not wishlists. Most people play 10 minutes and leave, but a few stick around, and those are gold. I made a Discord early and put the link in the game, so the ones who liked it had somewhere to report bugs. A couple of them still send me long lists every week.

The other thing that helped was anonymous stats in the game, just how far people got and where they stopped. People rarely tell you where they quit, but the numbers do. That's how I found my tutorial was too long.

And yeah, the redesigning never really ends. Just don't let it stop you from putting it out there.

replies.author: HazeInsanity
replies.body:
Thank you, your feedback is worth gold to me!

 [Itch.io](http://Itch.io) or discord could really help steer me in the right direction early in development. 

Good luck on your project, I'll keep an eye on it as well!

comments.author: SeaofColtrane
comments.body:
You probably can’t afford good artists but you can always shop around and see of you get lucky.

The key to making AI art look good is developing a unique art style and being very critical of what AI produces.

Personally you shouldn’t make your dream game or something big right off the bat. Get the 20 dollar Claude subscription, and start messing around with Opus 5.5 or whatever else. Make some small games, get the feel for it, then if you think you have a good idea, try to make something high quality.

replies.author: HazeInsanity
replies.body: Those are the exact steps I'm taking, glad to see I'm on the right track then. I have been using Opus 5.5 and It has been doing pretty well. I'm taking my time making sure the sprites and art I'm using is pretty consistent, animations have been the biggest hurdle so far and I think I'll need other people's opinions on it

replies.author: SeaofColtrane
replies.body: Animations definitely take a lot of work and user input. Keep at it and it’ll get better and better!
